title: Stay CALM: Calibrated Online Aggregation for Multi-Horizon Forecasting Under Delayed, Overlapping Feedback
abstract: Online time-series forecasters keep adapting after deployment, but a forecast for h steps ahead can only be scored h steps later, and forecasts issued at neighbouring times share most of their targets. We argue that this overlap, more than the delay itself, is what makes online adaptation fragile. The losses that reach an online learner at horizon h are serially correlated, their long-run variance is inflated by an overlap factor κ^h that grows roughly like h up to h ≈ 30 on most standard benchmarks, and learning rates chosen for independent feedback end up chasing noise. For fixed-share exponential weights, a diffusion analysis shows that the excess loss caused by this noise depends on the learning rate η only through ηκ^h. The resulting calibration has nothing to tune: divide the learning rate by κ^h, and let the switching rate grow with it. We build CALM, a two-level aggregator that applies the calibration to selection, linearised exponential weights and a second-order combiner. It uses only the forecasts of its experts, so it can sit on top of any forecasting models, open or closed source, including published online methods run in their authors’ code. Because every aggregate is a convex combination of the experts, any aggregation rule can be replayed exactly from stored error statistics, which lets us compare 45 rules on identical forecasts. In 75 development settings CALM was never worse than not adapting. In two pre-registered confirmatory rounds (90 runs) it had lower error than Proceed, a state-of-the-art leak-free method that is also one of its experts, in 88 runs (by 6.2% on average, 3.8% outside ETTh2). It is rarely the single best of the twelve methods we compare, but in no run was its error more than 3.5% above the best one, the smallest such margin among them. Calibrated BOA, one of its components, has the lowest error most often, and the tuning-free delayed learner AdaHedgeD is slightly better than CALM in most runs but fails badly in one recurring setting. CALM’s update takes about a millisecond per time step.
